speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Singapore is committed to the global fight against illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: As an international trading hub, we take this issue very seriously.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We are a signatory to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, or CITES in short.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: CITES ensures that international trade in wildlife and plants does not threaten their survival in the wild.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We have also put in place a whole-of-Government enforcement framework and we work closely with regional and international partners to stop illegal wildlife shipments from passing through our borders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Our efforts also helped the Chinese authorities to arrest 14 suspected criminals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Last August, we opened our Centre for Wildlife Forensics, to enhance our science and research capabilities, in collaboration with international partners and local experts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Recently, our studies with Prof Samuel Wasser from the University of Washington found that most of the large ivory seizures made globally over the past decade, came from repeated poaching at the same location and even from the same families of elephants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Such insights help us better understand the patterns and networks of illegal wildlife trade and we share them with our international partners to facilitate cross-border enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will help source countries to focus on tackling elephant poaching hotspots and the illegal export of ivory, and destination countries to curb consumer demand for ivory products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Centre for Wildlife Forensics was also recognised as a CITES Reference Laboratory in June.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This recognition is a testament to Singapore's capabilities in wildlife forensic science in supporting the implementation and enforcement of CITES.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It also attests to the high standards of the Centre in conforming to ISO quality assurance standards for wildlife forensic testing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: With this, we can help other CITES member states carry out wildlife forensic analyses, on top of sharing our experiences and expertise with them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will aid them in investigating and prosecuting illegal wildlife trade cases more easily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Together, we can strengthen our efforts against the criminal syndicates and networks that conduct illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: And within Singapore, we also continue to partner key stakeholders and the community to raise awareness on our roles in tackling illegal wildlife trade and protecting our planet's biodiversity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This includes regularly engaging industry stakeholders, such as the maritime industry, e-commerce companies and financial institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: And reaching out to the wider public through outreach and education programmes, such as webinars and exhibitions, to better understand their roles in tackling the illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, just this March, our volunteers under NParks' Youth Stewards for Nature Programme organised the World Wildlife Day Regional Youth Symposium, which brought youths around the ASEAN region together, to discuss ideas and solutions to tackle illegal wildlife trade in Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: These are some of the steps that we have taken to combat the threat of illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: But this threat is constantly evolving and because illegal wildlife trade is so profitable, smugglers are constantly looking for loopholes to exploit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: So, beyond strengthening our research capabilities, partnerships and engagements, we must ensure that our regulations and enforcement tools remain up-to-date and effective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Endangered Species (Import and Export) Act or ESA for short, is the key legislation that supports Singapore's regulation of trade in the wildlife species protected under CITES.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It gives us the powers to take enforcement action against illegal traders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In drafting these amendments, we consulted a wide range of partners and stakeholders, including traders, shipping companies, industry associations, academics and non-profit organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Last November, we also embarked on a public consultation on the ESA amendments and on Singapore's approach to combating illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We have carefully studied the feedback received and incorporated relevant suggestions in our amendments in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This includes additional amendments to make the Act more effective and more closely aligned with relevant domestic and international laws on endangered species.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This Bill seeks to amend ESA in four key areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: First, on our requirements for CITES species traded in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Currently, traders are required to produce a CITES permit or certificate when importing, transiting, exporting, or re-exporting CITES species in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This allows NParks to verify that the trade in these species is legal, sustainable, traceable and in line with CITES requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We are making amendments to ESA to provide greater clarity for all stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In particular, on the requirements for the transit of CITES species through Singapore and the documents required for such trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: First, we will amend the definition of "transit" in ESA to make clear when CITES species are considered to be in transit in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Today, ESA states that for a CITES species to be considered "in transit" in Singapore, the species, must among other things, be brought into Singapore solely for the purpose of taking it out of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We recognise that ESA could be clearer on how this "sole purpose" requirement is to be satisfied, such that there is no ambiguity on when species are considered "in transit".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Traders can provide a Bill of Lading, air waybill or sea waybill, which state the final destination of the CITES species transported.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: These are among standard transport documents used in international shipping today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: A list of the accepted documents will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Second, we will make clear the permits that traders need to obtain from the countries of export, re-export or import, for CITES species in transit in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Today, traders are required to produce CITES permits for CITES species transiting in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Where the countries of export, re-export or import are not CITES Parties, "written permission", which is not defined in the Act, can be produced instead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This is for NParks to verify that the species have been legally exported and will be accepted by the country of import.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: To ensure that NParks receives the information it needs for such verification, clause 4 makes it clear that the permits, certificates, or any other similar documents submitted must contain information that will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Where the countries of export, re-export or import are CITES Parties, traders should continue to present valid CITES permits or certificates containing the prescribed information to NParks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Where these countries are not CITES Parties, traders will be required to present valid permits, certificates or any other similar document containing the prescribed information to NParks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The prescribed information will include details of the competent authorities approving the export, re-export or import of the CITES species, as well as the scientific names, source and quantity of the specimens traded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: With these amendments, we aim to provide greater clarity on the requirements for the transit of CITES species in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Traders will not have to make significant changes to their existing business operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: But following these amendments, we will be better able to differentiate between CITES species which are meant for import into Singapore and species which are meant for transit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: NParks can then take appropriate enforcement action against those who illegally import or transit these CITES species.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The amendments will strengthen Singapore's existing strict stance against illegal trade in CITES species.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: CITES Resolutions provide guidance and recommendations on how CITES Parties should interpret and implement CITES rules and regulations on wildlife trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: As a responsible CITES Party, we follow the CITES Resolutions closely, where they apply to us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: At the same time, we continue to ensure that trade can flow freely and easily, so that we maintain our status as a global trade hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, NParks issues CITES permits for CITES species exported, re-exported or imported in Singapore in accordance with the permit requirements set out in the relevant CITES Resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This ensures that our permits are recognised and accepted by other CITES authorities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We are now amending ESA to ensure that our laws are even more closely aligned with these CITES Resolutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: These are animals whose recent lineage include species listed in CITES Appendices I or II, including species that are either threatened with extinction and species for which trade is regulated for their continued survival.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Taking the Bengal cat as an example, the Bengal cat is a cross between the wild Asian Leopard Cat, a CITES-listed species, and the domestic cat.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: CITES permits are required for the trade in Bengal cats, which have a wild Asian Leopard Cat ancestor in their lineages, up to four generations that precede it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Although ESA does not currently explicitly require this, our traders have been producing such permits when trading Bengal cats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 2 also makes clear that urine, faeces or ambergris are not regulated under ESA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: As these are waste products that are naturally excreted, their collection does not threaten the survival of any CITES species in the wild.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: That brings our regulations on the trade in animal parts or derivatives more in line with CITES's recommendations in this area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Retrospectively issued documents can only be accepted if the documents are for trade in CITES Appendix II or III species and the circumstances that led to the retrospective issuance were not caused or contributed to by the trader.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This amendment will strengthen enforcement against those who trade in CITES species without valid permits or other documents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We last enhanced the penalties under the Act in 2006.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: However, the value of smuggled endangered wildlife has continued to rise over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, in 2019, we seized a shipment of around 12 tonnes of pangolin scales that were worth over $48 million, as well as around nine tonnes of elephant ivory worth over $17 million.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Thus, after careful review and consultation with stakeholders and the public, and considering the latest domestic and international laws on endangered species, we will enhance our penalties further to keep pace with the times and to increase deterrence against illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We will increase the fines and jail terms that can be meted out for individuals who illegally trade in CITES species.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 4 also increases the maximum imprisonment term for the illegal trade in Appendix II and III species, from two years to four years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Wildlife trade offences in relation to Appendix I species have stiffer penalties as these species are threatened with extinction and the impact of illegal trade on their survival is much more severe.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We will also increase our penalties for the domestic trade in CITES species to align with that for international trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This means that individuals who illegally sell CITES species, such as rhino horns, tiger parts and elephant ivory in Singapore, will be subject to the same higher penalties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This is to enhance deterrence and reflect a similarly strict stance against the illegal domestic trade of endangered species.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Offenders that are corporations, unincorporated associations or partnerships who illegally trade CITES species will also be subject to higher penalties than individual offenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This is because such entities generally have more resources and the means to move larger quantities of illegally traded CITES species, compared to individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We will also introduce higher maximum imprisonment terms of eight years for Appendix I species and six years for Appendix II or III species, to penalise individuals within corporate offenders, such as directors or managers, more strictly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We will also raise the maximum aggregate fine further across the board, for both individual and corporate offenders, to match the market value of all illegally traded CITES species comprised in the offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This ensures that the penalties are proportionate to the potential gains from the illegal trade of such CITES species, which have risen over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, in 2020, a South African trader was sentenced to 17 months of jail for transiting through Singapore, from South Africa to Vietnam, with 22 kilograms of rhinoceros horns without a valid CITES permit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: At the same time, clause 10 will amend section 17 to penalise any person who misleads the authorities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Today, ESA only penalises false, but not misleading statements or documents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, a trader applying for an import permit may deliberately mislead NParks officers by providing once-legitimate supporting documents that have since been revoked by the document issuer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: These changes will enhance our ability to take enforcement action under the Act against individuals or entities who mislead the authorities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Apart from these enhancements, the Bill also provides greater clarity to existing penalties in the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Currently, the Act provides for fines for illegal trade offences to be issued for each CITES species.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This is currently defined to mean any animal or plant specified in the Schedule of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 4 does not change the current position, but makes it clear that that the fines are levied on a per specimen basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In other words, the offender would be fined on the basis of each specimen of the CITES species, such as each piece of rhinoceros horn or elephant ivory, comprised in the offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Taken together, these revisions to the penalties will serve as a strong deterrent and enforcement against illegal trade in wildlife.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Lastly, the Bill will also make other changes to clarify and strengthen NParks' enforcement powers, and facilitate investigations on illegal wildlife trade offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: First, the amendments will enhance NParks' powers to seize items under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, if NParks seizes a shipment of non-CITES timber planks, with illegally traded elephant ivory concealed beneath those planks, the current ESA only allows NParks to seize the elephant ivory.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 6 makes clear that NParks may also seize items that are used to conceal CITES species, in this case, the timber planks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In addition, under clause 9, conveyances, such as cars and vans, that were used to commit a wildlife trade offence may also be seized.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: These changes will further deter against illegal wildlife trade as would-be smugglers would stand to lose their vehicles, as well as any additional cargo that was used to commit the offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Nonetheless, we recognise that there must be safeguards to the expanded powers in respect of conveyances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: In addition, the Courts may only order the forfeiture of other conveyances, if a person was convicted of an offence under the Act and the conveyance was used in the commission of the offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Clause 9 also introduces amendments to the forfeiture framework in ESA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Currently, ESA allows the mandatory forfeiture of CITES species and other items upon conviction for illegal wildlife trade offences under sections 4 or 5 of the Act today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This will also apply to any offence under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The Bill also updates provisions to align the Act with other recent legislation, including the Wildlife Act, which came into force in 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, clause 12 will introduce protections against liability for NParks' authorised officers, if they have acted in good faith and with reasonable care in the execution of any power or performance of any function, under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: At the same time, the amendments will enhance NParks' operational efficiency and investigative capabilities, as well as facilitate its prosecutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, clause 8 will allow NParks' authorised officers to be accompanied or assisted by persons, such as Auxiliary Police Officers, in their inspections, searches and seizures of premises or shipments of goods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: NParks' authorised officers will also be allowed to dispose of perishable seized items, such as turtle eggs, under clause 6, to avoid incurring unnecessary storage and maintenance costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Relatedly, clause 12 allows for documents produced by authorised NParks officers, to be admissible as evidence and taken as factual unless proven otherwise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Lastly, clause 12 will insert new protection for informers by allowing for non-disclosure of information during the Court proceedings that might lead to the identification of an informer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This is to encourage persons to provide information regarding illegal wildlife trade, given that NParks often relies on tip-offs to enforce against illegal wildlife trade and smuggling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: It reflects our firm commitment to tackle the global issue of illegal wildlife trade, as a Party to CITES.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The amendments will enable us to continue taking effective action against illegal wildlife trade, as it evolves over time, for example, from brick-and-mortar to virtual markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: This included several CITES species, such as the Burmese Python and tarantulas that had been illegally imported.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: We will continue to monitor and enforce against the sale of illegally imported CITES species, which will in future be subject to heavier penalties under the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: The amendments are also largely aimed at strengthening NParks' enforcement against illegal wildlife trade – the smugglers and errant traders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: And, any offence made out under the Act will depend on the investigation findings of each case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For the large majority of the industry, who have been responsibly following the requirements in the trade of CITES species, the amendments will have minimal impact on the existing processes or business operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: And, we thank you for your cooperation and for doing your part to safeguard our earth's natural heritage and environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Everyone can play a part in combating illegal trade in wildlife and in protecting our planet's biodiversity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: For example, when buying a pet, do patronise licensed pet shops, ask the sellers for a CITES permit if you are buying a CITES species, such as dragonfish or sulphur-crested cockatoo.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Do also refrain from buying items which may contain endangered animal or plant parts, or illegal wildlife products, such as elephant ivory.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: Together, we can reduce the demand for endangered wildlife and contribute towards stopping illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Minister for National Development)
text: And in partnership with the international community, we will continue to play our part to safeguard earth's natural heritage – not just for ourselves, but also for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have had the privilege to be involved since the first draft of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know that MND has made many changes to reflect feedback from NGOs and other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no doubt that today's Bill helps.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the public consultation found, there is consensus that harsher, broader penalties does deter the illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, this Bill does not do enough to tackle the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is a need to rethink the broader policy approach towards tackling this illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In its first undercover investigation conducted back in 2001, ACRES found that 73.5% of shops surveyed in Singapore were illegally selling bear bile and bear gall bladders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some may say this is just the sale of goods to willing buyers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen the suffering that fuels this market.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first bear I met lived her life in a cage not bigger than herself.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She was stabbed into her gall bladder so that they could drain the bile from her every single day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first bear I met in a bear farm is also the first bear that I watch passed away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She took her last breath before my very eyes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Over the past 20 years, I’ve seen many other animals in similar conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen monkeys restrained with chains so tight that it bit into the flesh of their neck, chains that were never loosened as the animals grew over the years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many people think Singapore has little to do with this suffering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is they could not be more wrong.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore is a critical nexus in the illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the past decade, we have seized illegal shipments of animal parts worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Elephants, rhinoceroses, pangolins – these are just a few animals whose dead, dissected bodies are smuggled through Singapore's world-class port.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just a week later, we seized another 12.7 tonnes of pangolin scales.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just a few weeks ago, a man was arrested in South Africa for attempting to carry 26 kilogrammes of rhinoceros horns into Singapore in his hand luggage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such seizures are just the tip of the iceberg.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Smugglers have found ways to circumvent our border security and bring these animals and their body parts onto our soil.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore can and needs to do much more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In practice, this means amending OCA so that it considers offences under sections 4, 5 and 19 of ESA and sections 8 and 9 of the Wildlife Act as serious offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For so long, our policy framework on the illegal wildlife trade has targeted the runners, the low-level criminals carrying the goods.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But my proposal attacks the heart of the problem: the syndicate leaders, the masterminds making everything happen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Including wildlife trade offences in OCA gives the authorities more tools to investigate and punish these kingpins, who today may evade punishment under the ESA framework.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we debated in this House previously, a lot of the people we prosecute under ESA are the runners, not the kingpins.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just as important, it lets us follow and cut off the money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under OCA, our officers can issue financial reporting orders to get information and then use civil confiscation regime to deprive syndicates of their financial gains.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Minister for Home Affairs has said that to classify an offence under OCA, the offence must meet two criteria.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It must pose a serious threat to public safety and security in Singapore, and it must be associated with organised crime in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Wildlife trafficking clearly meets the first requirement: it poses a significant threat to our public safety and security.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Wildlife traffickers operate outside the scrutiny of our health officials.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This makes the animals they transport more likely to spread zoonotic diseases to humans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: COVID-19 is a zoonotic disease and so is monkeypox.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do not think I need to dwell further on how dangerous zoonotic diseases are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Animals brought into Singapore in an unregulated way may become invasive species that threaten our native wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Javan myna we see every day is an excellent example.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Brought in via the caged bird trade, they have been threatening the survival of native birds like the oriental magpie-robin and the common myna who is not so common anymore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) reports that wildlife crime cases have been connected with offences, such as corruption, drug trafficking and money laundering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Failing to effectively tackle illegal wildlife trade in Singapore may also increase our risk of our financial institutions and trade systems being abused to facilitate other serious crimes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does wildlife trafficking meet the second requirement of being associated with organised crime in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When you look at the size and value of the animal-part seizures at our borders, we are talking about operations that must, by logic, involve financing, coordinating and operations on a large, organised scale.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A $50 million shipment of pangolin scales is not the work of isolated individuals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, the FATF describes the illegal wildlife trade as a "major transnational organised crime", run by highly organised criminal syndicates that engage in complex fraud.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Minister for Home Affairs has said that the 18 cases of wildlife crime we prosecuted have not been found to be associated with organised crime in Singapore or overseas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The statistic merely points to the need for greater investigative powers, particularly those provided under OCA, which will help connect instances of wildlife trafficking to their kingpins.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the direct benefits of catching criminals, there is a reputational benefit for including the ESA offences under OCA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has always prided itself as a global financial hub.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it has come under criticism by FATF, which has said Singapore is insufficiently focused on complex, transnational cases of money laundering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Separately, FATF has called for countries to provide their agencies with the mandate and tools to conduct financial investigations into the illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Including ESA under OCA would thus benefit us by addressing FATF's concerns, allowing us to meet international standards to combat money laundering and improving our reputation both as a financial hub and a key fighter against wildlife crime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: From the start of this month, FATF will have its first Singaporean President, Mr T Raja Kumar.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With the first Singapore presidency of FATF, I hope we can build on FATF's focus on tackling the financial trails of illegal wildlife trade internationally.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On the national level, we can do better in strengthening our organised crime laws to tackle illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This move was widely reported and globally praised, with many organisations affirming the amendment as the "most appropriate route to effectively combat wildlife crime".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On behalf of NGOs and law professors in Singapore, I have submitted a position paper on including illegal wildlife trade offences under ESA and the Wildlife Act to the Organised Crime Act to Senior Minister of State Mr Tan Kiat How.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The paper was prepared together with the NGOs, lawyers and law professors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to working together with Senior Minister Tan and MHA to see how we can move forward on this proposal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad the Bill recognises the importance of informers in policing wildlife crimes by granting them protection under the new section 22B.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Smugglers use creative strategies, complicated trade routes and fraudulent documents to avoid detection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, one of the shipments of pangolin scales was caught and was packed and declared as frozen beef.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I imagine it cannot be possible for us to fully scrutinise every single shipment of frozen beef passing through Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Informers are thus an important asset to assist our enforcement agents in their work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to incentivise informers to come forward and make reports.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can do this by allowing informers to be rewarded by our fines imposed under ESA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is similar to what is done under section 13 of the Wildlife Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third proposal is to increase the maximum aggregate fine for offences under ESA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill does make a progressive step of increasing the limits of fine to the market value of the specimens involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The illegal wildlife trade is a hugely profitable enterprise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Successfully smuggling pangolin scales or elephant ivory earns these criminals millions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need penalties that really hurt the profits of the syndicates or it would not be enough to deter them from using Singapore for their operations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would make the fines in a genuine penalty similar to the civil penalty for insider trading, tax evasion or illegal customs drawback claims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My last proposal is that we make buying scheduled species an offence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As long as there is a domestic market, smugglers will always try to bring in animals illegally.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2019, when I asked about our efforts to deter the pangolin trade in Singapore, Minister of State Sun Xueling acknowledged that tackling the illegal wildlife trade requires buyers to reduce their demand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is nice that she just stepped in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know buying is currently already an offence but it is not explicitly stated in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should be explicit by stating clearly in the Bill that it is an offence to buy scheduled species.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We would be following in the footsteps of many other countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Legislation in the US, EU, Brunei, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam already include “purchasing” as an offence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This was a speech by HRH Prince William at the 2018 Illegal Wildlife Trade Conference in London which I had the privilege to attend.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: HRH shared how, on his visit to Africa, he saw rhinos under such threat that they had more bodyguards than him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He said, quote: “It is heart-breaking to think that by the time my children George, Charlotte and Louis are in their twenties, elephants, rhinos and tigers might well be extinct in the wild.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is carried out by ruthless cross-border criminal networks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It undermines governance and the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It robs communities today of their future sources of income.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And it exploits the poorest people in some of the most vulnerable countries on earth.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They see it as a lucrative and relatively low-risk activity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are the very same groups who move drugs, people and weapons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These networks are sophisticated, coordinated, adaptable and professional.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They innovate faster than we can and they exploit weaknesses in our systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know very well that law enforcement resources and judicial systems are stretched.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I am asking you to see the connections.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And to recognise that this is a transnational crime that you cannot leave to your passionate, but thinly stretched, wildlife crime officers to tackle alone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Remember – "Al Capone was convicted of tax evasion, not murder." I hope we will remember this powerful speech by HRH Prince William as we increase our efforts in tackling this cruel and wasteful illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.35 pm until 5.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The depletion of biodiversity at commercial scales is contributing to the deterioration of biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services, posing a long-term threat to the well-being of humanity, as noted in the 2019 report of the Inter-governmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is broad international consensus about the widespread harm caused by the illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Governments must do what they can to deter such crimes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Developed nations like Singapore have an even greater responsibility in this regard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We owe it to the world to crack down hard on these criminal enterprises.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rightfully, Singapore has been a party to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) since 1986.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This region is also an entryway into China, reportedly the world’s largest consumer market for illegal wildlife products.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our highly developed trade infrastructure and global connectivity are prone to exploitation to facilitate illicit activities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The ESA Bill was read for the first time on 9 May this year and was initiated to amend the 2006 Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I support this Bill as a step in the right direction, but in my speech I shall raise a number of suggestions on how the regulatory regime applicable to the wildlife trade can be further strengthened with a view to stamping out the trade in endangered species.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The amendments acknowledge updates to CITES protocols and definitions and, concurrently, update the law.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Definitions pertaining to import/export, the items being traded, as well as the documentation required to validate this trade, have been clarified.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In addition, the Bill grants improved powers of enforcement to the National Parks Board or NParks, the agency responsible for implementing CITES regulations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It closes loopholes by explicitly not recognising retrospective CITES trade permits, granted, with certain exceptions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Singapore’s import/export laws must adapt to ensure that the wildlife trade is regulated sustainably and that the illegal wildlife trade, which is driven by organised crime, be dealt a body blow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I offer the following suggestions for future changes that could be made via legislation or perhaps subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In line with CITES regulations, exceptions to the import/export rules have been made for naturally excreted urine, faeces and ambergris.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, in a regional context, they represent exploitable loopholes that can allow unsustainable practices to persist.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, Kopi Luwak, or civet coffee, is typically sold as coffee beans excreted by civets from many Southeast Asian nations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In truth, this industry sometimes relies on inhumane wild-capture and forced feeding of civets, although I am not claiming that every Kopi Luwak producer engages in inhumane practices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is often difficult to identify if the resultant product is “naturally excreted" or not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As a result of these exceptions, the amended law does not afford these animals the protection they need.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I move on from this example, let me note that I am using the example of Kopi Luwak as an illustration.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Asian palm civet is not currently an endangered species and the issue I alluded to is related to cruelty towards animals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, the example illustrates a problem that may arise with endangered animal-derived products.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I will take the example of leopard cats and I believe Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How also referred to this example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They are classified under CITES Appendix II, which requires their trade to be controlled.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Their hybrids, with domestic cats, are known as Bengal cats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My understanding of the comments made by Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How earlier is that, currently, traders do voluntarily submit such documentation but it is my understanding that the Bill does not require such documentation to be submitted.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, that is a loophole that can perhaps be plugged.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such exceptions can allow local demand to drive poaching and captive breeding in other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should consider tweaks to the regulations that would require the spirit of CITES to be applied to hybrids in a reasonable manner, so as to deter such activities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Sir, in this Bill, penalties for infringements of the Bill have been increased.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This will, laudably, increase the deterrence against infringements of the law.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, one significant gap in the ESA Bill as it stands would appear to be the online wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An overwhelming share of the illegal wildlife trade is now carried out online.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A 2020 study found that more than a third of all reptile species were traded online.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Almost 90% of those species were caught from the wild, with many being rare and endangered.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are recent reports of exotic wildlife being sold as pets on social media in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should require online platforms to self-police the transactions they facilitate in this regard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The trade of species which are listed in the various appendices are regulated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, this still represents a small fraction of animals and plants on earth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Larger, more charismatic animals are disproportionately represented in these appendices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Species that are identified by experts and NGOs as being threatened by trade take many years to make it into CITES listings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Without such a listing, unregulated trade in wildlife is the default.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The current model of direct listing relies on customs agents to verify shipments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It places the burden of proof of trade sustainability onto the Government and on NGO watchdogs, while businesses profit from the trade.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Newly described species, those that have just been discovered and have just become known to science, newly discovered species which are usually unlisted, are left completely vulnerable to trade.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Why not, then, use a reverse-listing model which would make "no-trade" the default?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a system would require the traders themselves to produce proof of sustainable trade.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a system could also incorporate a default ban on newly discovered species for a certain period of time, so as to allow time for that species to be listed, if the facts so warrant.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What some scientists have dubbed the Anthropocene era – the era in earth’s history when human actions drive change in global climate and biological conditions – must not become the era of another mass extinction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rare and endangered species have a key role to play in keeping ecosystems in balance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Their bodies may contain keys to biopharmaceutical and other scientific breakthroughs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And they form part of the earth’s magnificent diversity, of which we are stewards and which should not be denied to future generations of human beings – and when I say that, I look up at the Gallery and I see many young students – very heartening to see that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In Asia, the problem is acute, as Asia is home to many endangered species while also being a major global centre of demand for endangered wildlife and wildlife products.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While public awareness of the plight of iconic species, such as the African Elephant and the Black Rhino, for example, is relatively high, many other less high-profile species are also prey to illegal wildlife markets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Post-pandemic, we expect the volume of imports and exports to increase substantially.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will correspondingly apply to the illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Southeast Asia is a hotspot for illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, we must stay vigilant and come down hard on illegal wildlife traders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, illegal wildlife trade should be recognised as serious organised crime.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Member Louis Ng raised this earlier as well.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: According to INTERPOL, wildlife crime is a part of serious organised crime, which feeds into money laundering, tax evasion and corruption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many other countries, including Hong Kong and the European Union, have also treated illegal wildlife trade as such.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In doing so, the relevant authorities are accorded greater enforcement powers to investigate the illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This enables them to effectively track down the heads of the syndicates through the money flows.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, we must do more to investigate and conduct enforcement of illegal wildlife trade happening in the digital realm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only a week ago, we read in the media of local Telegram groups being blatantly used to buy and sell exotic pets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are our Police, NParks or Customs closely monitoring such groups?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the possibility of identifying and arresting the perpetrators?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would the buyers be penalised, if they transacted with the seller but do not yet have the animal in possession?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would sellers be prosecuted as a business or commercial entity, even if they are not registered as a business?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would also be pertinent to find out how such traders could still bring in these exotic wildlife.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In recent years, INTERPOL updated its training syllabus to address ways to tackle digitally-enabled wildlife trafficking.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With increasing amounts of digital evidence recovered during wildlife crime investigations, digital forensics is high on the training agenda.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The emphasis that INTERPOL places on such skills among their crime investigative professionals is a testament to how widespread and severe the online wildlife trade problem is.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Besides social media platforms and messaging apps like Telegram, the dark web has also become an increasingly popular platform for wildlife trafficking syndicates to conduct their operations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do our local NGOs and agencies have the capabilities, training and resources to effectively track down these criminals in the digital realm?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need to hold online technology companies accountable for exposing wildlife crime and thwarting the sale of exotic pets online.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Digital Services Act by the European Parliament was recently amended to introduce new transparency requirements for companies that will make the detection of illegal wildlife products and law enforcement easier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It makes explicit reference to the illegal trade of animals in the definition of "illegal content".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In addition, it requires that service providers take quick and effective measures to remove illegal content from their services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to ensure that "what is illegal offline is illegal online".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry look into adopting similar measures?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, the legislative treatment with regards to wildlife management and relevant laws should be more holistic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Presently, there are two acts covering wildlife, namely, the Wildlife Act and ESA.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: ESA only covers animals listed under the CITES Convention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe there is scope to combine the two acts to remove existing overlaps, if any, and to streamline the clauses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, can we have ESA expanded to cover more than just CITES animals?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we must deter consumers from contributing to illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This should be done through public education and effective enforcement and heavier penalties for offenders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Government regulations prohibit the ownership of most species of wild animals as pets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, as mentioned earlier, we have local Telegram channels with people selling and seeking out exotic pets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even though NParks can enforce on buyers who have such wildlife in possession, we should perhaps consider indicating "buying or looking to buy" as an offence under the Act.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will deter consumption and widespread queries in these Telegram chat groups.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Last month, a video of a woman carrying an endangered African Crown Crane in Singapore went viral.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It was thought to be a runaway pet.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These make me question the severity of current penalties.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Under the Wildlife Act, there is a maximum fine of $10,000 and/or imprisonment of up to six months for first time offenders keeping prohibited wildlife as pets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister share more about the enforcement of this law?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there routine checks conducted for signs of illegally kept wildlife in potential areas such as around landed estates?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there people keeping certain exotic pets under a permit?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, are routine visits conducted to ensure that the animal is still being responsibly housed and not used for breeding?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to educate people on why they should not keep wildlife as pets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There have been several cases of wildlife being discreetly abandoned and released into our nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To create an effective public education programme, we should obtain an understanding of the degree of public awareness about owning exotic pets in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is it due to ignorance and assumption that they make easy pets?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are consumers aware that releasing non-native wildlife into our forests and nature reserves upset our biodiversity and have adverse consequences on our ecosystem?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The adverse consequences of wildlife trade on public health deserves more prominence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Illegal wildlife trade fuels the spread of zoonotic diseases and pandemics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some of the most common and deadliest human diseases are caused by bacteria and viruses of animal origin, including COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have experienced first-hand the terrible consequences of a pandemic on lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must do everything within our means to stop or at least slow down the next one.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am confident that we can do more to utilise our capabilities in this area.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet the market for such pointless indulgences is built at the expense of needless immense suffering of living creatures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As Singapore moves towards a more compassionate and kinder society, we should not only encourage mutual care and concern amongst the people but also speak up and do more for the voiceless.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: First, on the proposed penalties for illegal wildlife trade in ESA.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Members, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Leon Perera and Mr Yip Hon Weng all have observed that that the illegal wildlife trade can make for very lucrative business and asked if the penalties for illegal wildlife trade could therefore be further enhanced to increase deterrence.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, by raising the proposed imprisonment term for individuals who illegally trade Appendix II or III species from four to five years, as suggested by Mr Yip Hong Weng, and increasing the maximum aggregate fine further across the board to three times the market value of the goods.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: First, I agree with Members on the need for adequate penalties.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will also introduce stiffer penalties for corporate offenders who illegally trade CITES species.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, you can see that we are taking significant steps in raising the penalties from the current Act, while also providing greater clarity to existing penalties such as specifying that the offender will be fined on the basis of each specimen of the CITES species comprised in the offence.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the same time, we need to strike the right balance, by ensuring that the penalties meted out are proportionate to the offence and consistent with our domestic legislation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, we have proposed higher penalties in this Act as compared to the Wildlife Act that Mr Yip Hon Weng mentioned which covers common wildlife.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is in view that illegal trade in CITES species has a significantly higher impact on the survival of these endangered species in the wild.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In addition to pegging the maximum aggregate fine to the market value of the goods, we have also proposed a maximum aggregate fine of $1,000,000 for corporate offenders.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This allows the Courts the flexibility to consider other aggravating factors and to impose much heavier penalties in cases where the market value of the goods is low.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This cap for the maximum aggregate fine for corporate offenders is proportionate to other serious offences in our domestic legislation, for example, the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act, where corporate offenders may be subject to a fine of $1,000,000 or twice the value of the benefits reaped from offences such as drug dealing.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Moreover, it is not just about consistency with our domestic legislation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Importantly, ESA gives effect to our commitment as a CITES party.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It touches on Singapore's obligation as a CITES party to combat illegal wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As cited by Mr Leon Perera, we have indeed benchmarked our proposed penalty framework against neighbouring jurisdictions in the region.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Our penalties will be roughly on par with our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, the proposed range of four to eight years for the maximum imprisonment terms for illegal wildlife trade offences is comparable to Malaysia, whose maximum imprisonment is up to seven years.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It also places Singapore on the middle end of the spectrum regionally.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Myanmar impose a maximum imprisonment term of up to 10 to 15 years, albeit with a significantly much lower monetary fine compared to our framework.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Meanwhile, in Cambodia, Laos and Indonesia, the maximum imprisonment terms are up to five years.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, we are not the lowest – compared with our neighbouring jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have introduced differentiated heavier penalties for offences involving CITES Appendix I species, which is also aligned to jurisdictions such as Brunei, the Philippines and Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This will serve to further deter illegal wildlife trade as would-be smugglers would face the prospect of losing their vehicles as well as any additional cargo that was used to commit the offence.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In a nutshell, we are taking steps to significantly raise the penalties.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the same time, we are mindful that the penalties need to be proportionate to the offence and are broadly consistent with other domestic legislation as well as comparable with our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Members have also pointed out that it would be important to reduce consumer demand for illegally traded CITES species by targeting buyers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This was also a suggestion raised during our public consultation exercise, which we have considered carefully.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Although "buying" is not explicitly set out as an offence in our legislation, Mr Yip Hon Weng has also pointed out there are other levers that penalise buyers of illegally traded CITES species.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And NParks has taken enforcement action using these levers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, under section 4 of ESA, any person in possession of a CITES species that has been illegally imported is guilty of an offence.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This includes possession of such a species purchased from a seller.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Under section 19 of ESA, any persons who abets the commission of any offence under ESA is also guilty of an offence.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This means that buyers can be penalised for facilitating the sale of illegally traded CITES species, including CITES species that cannot be sold, such as elephant ivory and rhinoceros horns.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the same time, we are mindful that there may also be persons who are unsuspecting purchasers of illegally traded CITES species.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Most of the general public might not be able to differentiate between CITES species and non-CITES species, much less be able to verify if the species was traded legally.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Hence, we aim to tackle this issue upstream.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: NParks conducts regular checks on businesses and individuals who sell CITES species to ensure that they have the relevant permits for the species.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These online sellers did not have the relevant permits for the CITES species.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, I would like to assure Members that we are paying close attention to such illegally traded CITES species on online platforms, including e-commerce platforms.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if online sellers would be prosecuted as a business or commercial entity even if they did not have a business registration.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In the case that I just mentioned, based on NParks' investigations, the online sellers were persons who were keeping the wildlife as pets or breeding them at home for sale.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They are individuals with no registered businesses and will be dealt with accordingly under ESA.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Also, in response to Mr Yip's comments, I would like to clarify that there are CITES species that can be kept as pets in Singapore but only with permission and the relevant permits from NParks.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Whether CITES species can be kept as pets is based on several factors, including the potential impact to animal and public health, animal welfare, environmental impact and public safety.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: NParks regularly reviews the suitability of these wildlife species as pets.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, apart from regulating the wildlife trade in Singapore, we also regulate the keeping of wildlife as pets to safeguard animal health and welfare.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We also aim to maintain a balanced ecosystem, which can be disrupted when non-native wildlife is illegally abandoned or released into our green and blue spaces.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: NParks receives tip-offs and monitors online and social media platforms for cases of illegally kept wildlife and will not hesitate to take strict action.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is in addition to our work with enforcement agencies and the industry to ensure that all CITES species are legally traded in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Our partnerships also play an important role to enhance our measures to combat illegal wildlife trade, including to bolster our capabilities to effectively tackle new forms of illegal wildlife trade, such as the recent shift of the trade on to online platforms, as Mr Yip Hon Weng highlighted.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Today, NParks works closely with the industry, such as e-commerce platforms and online auction houses, to combat the illegal trade of CITES species online.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested we hold the digital platforms accountable for removing content advertising and facilitating the sale of illegally traded CITES species.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We regularly engage these platforms to raise awareness on the impacts of illegal wildlife trade and educate these stakeholders on how they can contribute to our efforts to prevent the online trade of these products.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Thus far, the industry has been cooperative and committed to prevent the illegal sale of these products on their platforms.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
